passages.text: Dishwasher detergents clean dishes through a combination of chemistry, heat, and mechanical action. Their ingredients loosen food residues, break down grease and proteins, prevent minerals in water from interfering with cleaning, and help keep removed dirt from settling back onto dishes. Meanwhile, the dishwasher sprays water across the load, carrying away the loosened material. Unlike hand dishwashing liquids, which typically rely heavily on foam and are designed for use in a sink, automatic dishwasher detergents are formulated to work in a machine with controlled water temperatures, powerful spray jets, and relatively little foam. Their effectiveness depends on how several ingredients work together throughout the wash cycle. What happens when dishwasher detergent meets dirty dishes? Food residues can cling to dishes in different ways. Grease forms a water-resistant film, dried starch can create a stubborn coating, proteins from foods such as eggs and meat can adhere to surfaces, and mineral deposits can leave cloudy spots. No single cleaning ingredient handles all these materials equally well. When a dishwasher begins its wash cycle, water dissolves the detergent and distributes its active ingredients throughout the machine. In a dishwasher, the opposite happens: the dishes and cutlery stay still in plastic baskets while pressurized jets of hot water shoot all around them. Why detergent form and dosage matter Automatic dishwasher detergents come in powders, gels, and tablets or packs. These forms differ in how their ingredients are combined and released, but the basic cleaning principles are similar. Powders allow manufacturers to blend dry cleaning agents and may let users adjust the amount added. Gels contain ingredients in a liquid formulation. Tablets and packs provide a premeasured dose and may combine multiple components intended to dissolve or act at different stages of the cycle. The form alone does not determine cleaning performance. Ingredient composition, water hardness, the wash program, and the type of food residue all influence the result. Using too little detergent can leave insufficient cleaning ingredients to handle the load, particularly when dishes are heavily soiled or the water is hard. Using more than the recommended amount does not necessarily improve cleaning. The result depends on the detergent and dishwasher, and excessive dosing can contribute to residue or other unwanted effects. Without effective starch removal, a dish may retain a sticky or cloudy film even after the visible food has disappeared. Some formulations also use lipases, which break down fats into smaller components. Their contribution depends on the detergent formulation and the conditions inside the dishwasher. Enzymes are selective rather than universal cleaners. A protease does not perform the same job as an amylase, and neither is designed to dissolve every type of residue. Combining different enzymes allows a detergent to address a broader range of food soils. Temperature matters because enzymes are proteins with structures that determine how they work. Moderate heating can increase the rate of many enzyme-catalyzed reactions, but excessive heat can disrupt an enzyme’s structure and reduce its activity. Detergent manufacturers formulate enzyme systems to function under the conditions expected in a dishwasher’s wash cycle. Enzymes are particularly useful because they can break down complex food molecules without requiring the extreme temperatures or harsh chemical conditions that might otherwise be needed to achieve similar results. How hot does the water need to be? Dishwashers aim to strike a balance between speed, economy, and effectiveness. The hotter the water and the longer the wash, the more electricity you'll use and the more expensive each wash will be. In terms of hygiene, the hotter the water, the shorter the time you'll need to kill off any pathogens (bacteria and other nasties) lingering on your pots and pans. According to the [PDF] World Health Organization (summarizing a number of different scientific studies), water at temperatures close to that used in pasteurization (~60°C or 140°F) kills pathogens rapidly, with "inactivation times" ranging from a few seconds up to 30 minutes (depending on the pathogen). In other words, if your dishwasher is running at 60°C for 30–60 minutes, you can be fairly confident it's getting your things hygienically clean. Why some dishes still come out dirty A dishwasher’s performance depends on the interaction of chemistry, temperature, water movement, and the condition of the machine. When one of these factors is inadequate, food may remain even when the detergent is suitable. Dried-on starch and protein can be particularly difficult to remove if the wash conditions do not give enzymes enough opportunity to act. Grease may persist if the detergent solution does not reach the affected surface or if the water is not warm enough for the selected program. Hard-water deposits can create cloudy glassware even when food residues have been removed. Loading also affects cleaning. Dishes placed too closely together can block the spray, and large items can prevent water from reaching smaller ones. How rinse aids improve the final result Rinse aids serve a different purpose from the main detergent. They are released during the rinse stage, helping water spread more evenly across dish surfaces and drain away in sheets rather than remaining as separate droplets. This is especially useful because droplets of hard water can dry and leave mineral spots behind. By improving drainage, rinse aids reduce the amount of water left on surfaces to evaporate. They can also help dishes dry more effectively, depending on the materials being washed and the dishwasher’s drying method. Rinse aids do not replace the enzymes, alkaline ingredients, or other cleaning agents needed to remove food during the main wash. Instead, they improve the rinsing and drying stages after most of the soil has already been removed. Their benefits are often most noticeable on glasses, cutlery, and other smooth surfaces where water spots are easy to see.
